tasks.title: Why Owls Fly Quietly
tasks.text:
Most birds make a distinct swishing sound as they fly, produced by air rushing over their wings. Owls, however, are remarkably silent hunters, and this silence gives them a crucial advantage. Because many owls hunt at night and rely on hearing to locate prey, any noise from their own wings would mask the faint sounds of a mouse moving below. It would also alert the prey to the approaching danger.

Three features of owl feathers make near-silent flight possible. First, the leading edge of the wing is lined with stiff, comb-like structures that break up the air into smaller currents, reducing the turbulence that creates noise. Second, a soft fringe along the trailing edge smooths the air as it leaves the wing. Third, a velvety surface covers the feathers, absorbing the remaining high-frequency sound.

Together, these adaptations lower the noise of an owl's flight below the hearing range of a typical mouse. Engineers have studied these feathers closely, hoping to design quieter aircraft and wind turbines. So far, no artificial material has fully matched the owl's natural solution, though several designs inspired by it have reduced noise significantly.

tasks.intro: Listen to part of a talk in an environmental science class.
tasks.text:
Today I want to talk about a surprising kind of pollution — light pollution. When we think of pollution, we usually picture smoke or chemicals, but excessive artificial light at night is also a serious problem, and its effects reach far beyond spoiling our view of the stars.

Consider sea turtles. For millions of years, newly hatched turtles have found their way to the ocean by crawling toward the brightest horizon, which, on a natural beach, is the sea reflecting the moon and stars. But today, the glow of hotels and streetlights behind the beach is often brighter. As a result, hatchlings crawl inland, away from the water, where they die of exhaustion or are caught by predators.

Birds are affected too. Many species migrate at night and navigate by the stars. Bright city lights can disorient them, causing them to circle tall buildings until they collapse, or to collide with lit windows.

The good news is that light pollution is one of the easiest kinds of pollution to fix. Unlike carbon dioxide, light disappears the instant we switch it off. Simple steps — shielding lamps, using warmer colors, and turning off unnecessary lights — can make a real difference almost immediately.
